title: Climate Awareness and Community Resilience
subtitle: Understand how the climate is changing where you live and lead practical, measured actions that protect your household and community.
description: A practical beginner course on what climate change is, how it shows up across Nigeria, and how to measure and reduce your own household's vulnerability. You keep a local climate log, protect people from heat, track fuel and water, plant and care for trees, and finish with a documented community project and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Explain weather, climate and the greenhouse effect in plain language to your family or group
Score your household's vulnerability and name your top three climate risks
Keep a rainfall and temperature log and summarise it each month
Recognise heat illness, give correct first aid and run a heat check rota for at-risk neighbours
Measure a climate action with a baseline, indicators and percentage change
Plan and report a community resilience project with a 90-day plan
audience: Women and community leaders in Nigeria and across Africa who want to protect their households and neighbours from a changing climate, with no science background needed.
tools: A notebook and pen, or a notes app on your phone
A phone camera for evidence photos
A clear straight-sided container or a funnel and bottle for a rain gauge
A ruler and a kitchen measuring jug
A small hanging or kitchen scale for weighing fuel (optional)

modules.title: Understanding Climate Change Where You Live
modules.overview: You learn what climate change is and how it works, how it shows up in different parts of Nigeria, and how to measure your own household's vulnerability. By the end you have a family climate record, a local seasonal calendar and your top three vulnerabilities.

lessons.title: Weather, climate and the greenhouse effect: what is really changing
objectives: Explain the difference between weather and climate using a 30-year average
Describe the greenhouse effect in three plain sentences
Name the main human activities that add greenhouse gases
Tell adaptation, mitigation and resilience apart with a household example

blocks.text: People often say "the weather has changed". What they usually mean is that the **climate** has changed. The two words are different, and knowing the difference helps you read news, forecasts and your own experience correctly. **Weather** is what the sky and air are doing today or this week: rain this afternoon, a hot night, harmattan dust on Friday. **Climate** is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years: when the rains normally start, how hot March normally is, how long the dry season normally lasts.

How many years make a climate? The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations body for weather and climate, uses **30-year averages**, called climate normals, for example 1991 to 2020. One late rainy season is weather. Rains that arrive later, on average, across ten, twenty or thirty years show a change in climate.

blocks.name: white-sun-behind-cloud-with-rain
blocks.alt: A sun partly hidden behind a rain cloud
blocks.caption: Weather is today's sun and rain; climate is the pattern those days make over many years.

blocks.text: The greenhouse effect in plain words

Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground, the sea and our roofs. The warm ground then gives off heat back towards the sky. Some gases in the air, called **greenhouse gases**, hold part of that heat in, like a thick wrapper on a sleeping baby. Without them the Earth would be too cold for life. The problem is that people have added much more of these gases, so more heat is held in and the whole planet is warming.

blocks.title: How extra greenhouse gases warm the Earth
items: Sunlight warms the ground
Ground gives off heat
Greenhouse gases trap heat
More gases, more trapped heat
Warmer air and sea
blocks.caption: Each step follows from the one before: adding gases at step three is what pushes temperatures up.

blocks.text: According to the United Nations, human activities have been the main driver of climate change since the 1800s, mainly through burning **fossil fuels**: coal, oil and gas. The UN reports that the average temperature of the Earth's surface is now about **1.4°C warmer** than in the late 1800s. That sounds small, but it is an average over the whole planet, day and night, land and sea. A small rise in the average brings many more very hot days and heavier downpours.
Where the extra gases come from

head: Gas
Main human sources
Everyday example
rows: Burning coal, oil and gas; clearing land and cutting down forests
Petrol in a car, diesel in a generator, bush cleared and burned for a new farm
Agriculture, and oil and gas operations
Livestock and rice fields; gas released or flared at oil sites

blocks.text: Africa as a whole has added a small share of these gases compared with richer, industrialised regions, yet many African families feel the effects sharply because so much depends on rain: farming, water from wells and streams, and food prices in the market. That is why this course puts most of its weight on **coping and adapting**, while still showing the small cuts in emissions that also save money.
Three words you will use all through this course

items: **Adaptation**: changing how we live and work to reduce harm from a changing climate. For example, storing more water before the dry season or moving a shop's goods off the floor in the rainy season.
**Mitigation**: reducing the greenhouse gases we add, or taking them back out of the air. For example, using less charcoal or planting and protecting trees.
**Resilience**: the ability of a household or community to absorb a shock, such as a flood or a heatwave, recover quickly and come back stronger rather than poorer.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it weather or climate?
blocks.context: For example, Amina in a village near Bauchi has a family notebook in which her father wrote the date of the first rain good enough for planting each year. She counts days from 1 April (1 April = day 1) to compare years.
steps: Years 2016 to 2020: day 12 (12 April), day 25 (25 April), day 38 (8 May), day 19 (19 April), day 30 (30 April).
Average for these five years: (12 + 25 + 38 + 19 + 30) / 5 = 124 / 5 = 24.8, about day 25, which is 25 April.
Years 2021 to 2025: day 44 (14 May), day 33 (3 May), day 51 (21 May), day 40 (10 May), day 58 (28 May).
Average for these five years: (44 + 33 + 51 + 40 + 58) / 5 = 226 / 5 = 45.2, about day 45, which is 15 May.
Difference between the two averages: 45 - 25 = 20 days later.
She notices that 2018 (8 May) was late on its own, but the years after it went back to April. One late year is weather. A whole run of later years is a sign of a shifting pattern.
blocks.result: In her family's record, planting rains now arrive about 20 days later on average than five to ten years ago. Ten years is still shorter than WMO's 30-year normal, so Amina treats it as a strong local warning sign to plan around, not as final proof, and she keeps recording every year.

blocks.title: Your own records count
blocks.text: Official weather stations are far apart. A family notebook with dates of first rains, floods, very hot spells and harvests is valuable local evidence. Start one this week, even if you can only fill in what you remember from last year.

Keep three ideas from this lesson: climate is the long average, not one bad day; extra greenhouse gases from human activity are warming the planet; and your household can respond in two ways at once, by adapting to what is already happening and by cutting waste that adds to the problem.

takeaways: Weather is short-term; climate is the average pattern over about 30 years
Greenhouse gases trap heat; burning coal, oil and gas and cutting forests add more of them
The UN reports the Earth's surface is about 1.4°C warmer than in the late 1800s
Adaptation reduces harm, mitigation reduces emissions, resilience is bouncing back stronger
A family record of first-rain dates can reveal local change

activity.title: Start your family climate notebook
steps: Take a notebook or open a notes page on your phone and title it "Our climate record".
Ask one older family member for the month the rains usually started and ended when they were young.
Write down this year's first planting rain date, or your best memory of it, and last year's.
Add any very hot spells, floods or long dry spells you remember from the last three years, with the month.
Write one sentence in your own words explaining weather versus climate.
activity.evidence: A photo of your first notebook page with at least five dated entries and your one-sentence explanation

lessons.title: Reading climate signals in Nigeria's zones and in your own area
objectives: Match the main climate concerns to Nigeria's broad ecological zones
Run a "then and now" seasonal calendar session with older residents
Calculate how much a local season has shifted from calendar answers
Separate a real local trend from a single unusual event

blocks.text: Climate change does not look the same everywhere. A woman in Sokoto, one in Makurdi, one in Enugu and one in Bayelsa will each notice different changes, because they live in different zones with different rains, soils and water sources. This lesson helps you place your own community on that map and then collect local evidence about what has actually shifted.

blocks.name: environmental-study
blocks.alt: A person studying plants and the environment closely
blocks.caption: Looking carefully at your own surroundings is the first step in understanding local climate change.

blocks.text: Broad zones and their main concerns

Nigeria runs from dry savanna and Sahel in the far north to rainforest and mangrove swamps in the south. The table gives the commonly reported concerns for each broad zone. Your own area may sit between two zones or have special features such as a river, a dam or hills.

head: Broad zone
Examples of states
Commonly reported concerns
rows: Sokoto, Kebbi, Katsina, Kano, Jigawa, Yobe, Borno
Very hot dry seasons, short and unreliable rainy seasons, long dry spells, land drying out and losing vegetation (desertification), dust
Niger, Kwara, Kogi, Benue, Nasarawa, Plateau, FCT
Late or false starts to the rains, dry spells in the middle of the season, river flooding along the Niger and Benue
Ogun, Ondo, Edo, Enugu, Anambra, Imo
Heavier downpours in short periods, flash and urban flooding, gully erosion that eats into land and roads, hot humid nights
Lagos, Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers, Akwa Ibom, Cross River
Coastal erosion, sea water reaching farmland and wells (saltwater intrusion), flooding from rain, rivers and tides

blocks.title: A false start
blocks.text: A **false start** is when early rains arrive, farmers plant, and then a long dry spell kills the seedlings. Many farmers now wait for two or three good rains and moist soil before planting. Your community's experience of false starts is important climate information.
The "then and now" seasonal calendar

Official data covers big areas. Older residents can tell you what has changed on your street or farm. A **seasonal calendar** is a simple chart of the twelve months on which people mark when things usually happen. You make two rows: **Then** (about 20 to 30 years ago) and **Now** (the last five years). Then you compare.

items: Invite three to six older people, including at least two women, for about 45 minutes. A women's meeting, church or mosque group, or market association works well.
Draw the twelve months across a large sheet of paper, or on the ground with sticks.
For the Then row, ask: When did the rains usually start? When did they end? When was the hottest time? When was water hardest to get? When was food scarce before harvest?
Mark each answer with a symbol: a drop for rain, a sun for heat, an empty pot for water shortage, an empty basket for hunger.
Repeat the same questions for the Now row.
Ask what people do differently now because of the changes. Write down every answer, including ones you disagree with.
Take a photo of the finished calendar and read the main points back to the group to check you understood.

blocks.title: Then and now in one community
items: Then (about 25 years ago)
Now (last five years)
blocks.caption: Placing the two rows side by side makes the shift in each season easy to see and count.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting the shift
blocks.context: For example, Esther ran a seasonal calendar session with five elders in a farming community in Benue. Their answers matched the comparison chart above.
steps: Then: rains from early April to mid October. Count the months: April, May, June, July, August, September, and half of October = about 6.5 months.
Now: rains from early May to early October. May, June, July, August, September = 5 months, plus a few days of October, so about 5 months.
Shortening of the rainy season: 6.5 - 5 = about 1.5 months.
Wells now dry about one month earlier (February instead of March), so the hard water period is about one month longer.
Elders also report two-week dry spells in July that they did not see before.
blocks.result: Esther's community now has a rainy season about a month and a half shorter, a longer water-scarce period and mid-season dry spells. These three points become her community's local climate signals, and she will compare them with the next official seasonal forecast.

blocks.text: Trend or one-off?

Memory can be strong for dramatic years and weak for ordinary ones. To avoid mistakes, check that **several people agree**, ask for **examples with years** ("the year of the big flood was the year my son was born"), and compare with any written records, like Amina's notebook in Lesson 1, or with official information. If only one person remembers a change, write it down but mark it as "to check".

blocks.title: Respect every answer
blocks.text: Some elders explain changes through faith or tradition. Listen respectfully and record what they say. You are collecting observations of what changed and when; you do not need to argue about causes during the session.
By the end of this lesson you should have your zone, a list of its common concerns, and three local signals in your own words, backed by your seasonal calendar.

takeaways: Climate concerns differ by zone: heat and drought in the north, rain timing in the middle belt, heavy rain and erosion in the south, sea and salt on the coast
A seasonal calendar compares Then and Now month by month
Count months to measure how much a season has shifted
Trust a change more when several people agree and can name years

activity.title: Run a mini seasonal calendar
steps: Find at least three older residents willing to talk for 30 to 45 minutes.
Draw twelve months with a Then row and a Now row.
Mark rain start, rain end, hottest period, water scarcity and food scarcity in both rows.
Count the shift in months for at least two items.
Write your three main local climate signals in one sentence each.
activity.evidence: A photo of the finished calendar and a note listing your zone and three local signals

lessons.title: Mapping your household's climate vulnerability: exposure, sensitivity and capacity
objectives: Define exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity with your own examples
Score five areas of household life for climate vulnerability
Identify your household's top three vulnerabilities
Plan one quick improvement to adaptive capacity

blocks.text: Two families can live on the same street, face the same dry spell, and come out very differently. One loses income and pulls a child out of school; the other has a hard month and recovers. The difference is **vulnerability**. In this course, vulnerability means how prone you are to harm. It depends on how **sensitive** you are and how much **capacity** you have to cope and adapt. Add **exposure**, whether the hazard reaches you at all, and you have a simple tool for your own household.
The three parts

items: **Exposure**: does the climate hazard reach this part of your life? A shop on low ground is exposed to flooding; one on a hill is less exposed.
**Sensitivity**: if it reaches you, how badly does it hurt? A family whose only income is a rain-fed maize farm is very sensitive to a late rainy season. A salaried worker is less sensitive.
**Adaptive capacity**: what do you have that helps you cope and adjust? Savings, a second income, stored water, a strong group, information, skills and good health all add capacity.

blocks.name: house-with-garden
blocks.alt: A small house with a garden
blocks.caption: Your home, water, food, income and health each carry their own climate risks.

blocks.text: A five-area scoring sheet

Look at five areas of household life: **water, food, income, health and housing**. For each, give three scores from 1 to 3. Exposure: 1 low, 3 high. Sensitivity: 1 low, 3 high. Capacity gap: 1 if you are well prepared, 3 if you have little to fall back on. Add the three scores. Totals run from 3 to 9. The higher the total, the more vulnerable that area is.

blocks.title: Sensitivity against capacity
items: Sensitive, strong capacity: maintain
Sensitive, weak capacity: act first
Less sensitive, strong capacity: fine
Less sensitive, weak capacity: build slowly
blocks.caption: Areas that are highly sensitive and have weak capacity are where your first effort should go.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's scoring sheet
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi lives in Onitsha with her husband and four children. She sells provisions from a lock-up shop near a drain, and the family buys most of its food.
steps: Water: they buy water from vendors and store one drum. Exposure 2 (dry season raises prices), sensitivity 2, capacity gap 2. Total 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Food: all food is bought, and prices rise when harvests fail elsewhere. Exposure 2, sensitivity 3, capacity gap 2 (no food stock). Total 7.
Income: the shop is beside a drain that overflows in heavy rain; goods sit on the floor. Exposure 3, sensitivity 3, capacity gap 3 (no savings set aside). Total 9.
Health: hot nights in a room with one window; her mother, aged 70, stays with them. Exposure 3, sensitivity 2, capacity gap 3. Total 8.
Housing: the house is on higher ground and the roof is sound. Exposure 1, sensitivity 2, capacity gap 2. Total 5.
Ranking: income 9, health 8, food 7, water 6, housing 5.
blocks.result: Ngozi's top three vulnerabilities are: (1) flood damage to shop stock, (2) heat stress for her elderly mother at night, and (3) food price rises after poor harvests. She will tackle the shop first, because it scored highest and also feeds the family.

blocks.text: Quick wins that raise capacity

Some improvements cost little and move a score down quickly. Ngozi can raise her goods off the shop floor on pallets or blocks before the rainy season, clear the drain in front with her neighbours, and start a small weekly saving in her esusu or ajo group for emergencies. For her mother, she can improve night airflow and arrange a daily check during hot spells (Module 2 shows how).

head: Area
Example quick win
Score it lowers
rows: A second covered container filled before the dry season
Buying a bag of a dry staple at harvest time when prices are lower, stored safely
Raising stock off the floor; a small emergency saving
Knowing heat danger signs and checking on older relatives
Clearing gutters and drains before the rains

blocks.title: Be honest, not hopeful
blocks.text: Score what is true today, not what you plan to do. An honest score of 9 that leads to action protects your family more than a hopeful 5 that leaves the problem hidden.

blocks.title: Include everyone in the house
blocks.text: Ask other household members to score with you. Children may notice that their school route floods; an older relative may feel the heat more than you do. Their views change the scores.
Keep your scoring sheet. Your top three vulnerabilities are the first part of your capstone project, and you will rescore at the end of the course to see what moved.

takeaways: Vulnerability combines exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity
Score water, food, income, health and housing from 3 to 9
Your top three totals are your top three vulnerabilities
Cheap actions such as raising stock, clearing drains and small savings raise capacity fast

activity.title: Score your household
steps: Copy the five areas into your notebook with columns for exposure, sensitivity, capacity gap and total.
Score each area honestly with at least one other household member.
Add the totals and rank the five areas.
Write your top three vulnerabilities in one sentence each.
Choose one quick win for the top area and set a date to do it.
activity.evidence: Your completed scoring sheet with totals, top three vulnerabilities and one dated quick win

quiz.q: Bolanle's area had one very late rainy season this year after nine normal years. What is the best description?
options: A weather event; a climate change shows as a shift in the average over many years
Proof the climate has permanently changed
A sign that greenhouse gases have stopped rising
quiz.explain: Climate is the long-term average, usually over 30 years. One late year is weather, though it is still worth recording in your notebook.

quiz.q: Which activity adds the most to the greenhouse effect in this course's examples?
options: Burning fossil fuels such as petrol, diesel and coal
quiz.explain: The UN names burning coal, oil and gas as the main human driver of climate change, together with clearing forests.

quiz.q: A family builds a raised platform so their grain stays dry during floods. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Adaptation means changing how you live or work to reduce harm from climate impacts.

quiz.q: In a seasonal calendar, elders say rains used to run from early April to mid October; now they run from early May to early October. By about how much has the rainy season shortened?
quiz.explain: Then about 6.5 months, now about 5 months: 6.5 - 5 = about 1.5 months.

quiz.q: Ngozi scores her income area: exposure 3, sensitivity 3, capacity gap 2. What is the total and what does it mean?
options: 8, high vulnerability that should be near the top of her list
quiz.explain: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 out of a possible 9, so this area is highly vulnerable.

quiz.q: Which change lowers a household's capacity gap rather than its exposure?
options: Moving a shop to higher ground
Building a weekly emergency saving in an esusu group
Clearing the drain beside the house
quiz.explain: Savings add capacity to cope. Moving or clearing drains reduce exposure to the hazard itself.

modules.title: Practical Tools: Climate Records, Heat Safety and Measuring Change
modules.overview: You build a rain gauge and keep a local climate log, learn to protect the people most at risk from heat, and set up honest indicators to measure whether your household actions work. Each lesson ends with something you can use the same week.

lessons.title: Keeping a local climate log: a homemade rain gauge and daily temperature readings
objectives: Build and place a simple rain gauge correctly
Convert a funnel gauge's water volume into millimetres of rain
Summarise a month of readings: total rain, rainy days and longest dry run
Compare your log with the seasonal forecast terms onset, cessation and dry spell

blocks.text: Memories and elders' stories show the big picture. A daily log shows exactly what is happening this season. With a plastic container, a ruler and two minutes each morning, you can measure rainfall in **millimetres (mm)**, the same unit used by weather services. Over a few seasons, your log becomes a record your community can trust.

blocks.name: cloud-with-rain
blocks.alt: A grey cloud with falling rain
blocks.caption: Each millimetre of rain you record adds to a local record no weather station far away can give you.

blocks.text: What 1 mm of rain means

Rainfall is measured as the depth of water that would stand on flat ground if none soaked in, ran off or dried up. If rain fills a straight-sided container to 12 mm deep, then 12 mm of rain fell. The width of the container does not matter, as long as the sides are straight up and down and the bottom is flat. A wider container simply catches more water, spread over a wider base, so the depth is the same.
Two ways to build a gauge

items: **Straight-sided gauge (simplest):** a clear plastic jar or container with straight sides and a flat bottom, at least 10 cm wide. Measure the water depth with a ruler held upright from the inside bottom. Read in millimetres.

**Funnel gauge (better for small rains):** a funnel on top of a bottle catches rain over the funnel's mouth and keeps it from evaporating. Measure the water in millilitres (ml) with a kitchen measuring jug or marked feeding bottle, then convert to mm with the formula below.

blocks.text: The funnel formula: **rain in mm = water in ml ÷ funnel opening area in square centimetres × 10**. Find the area with **3.14 × radius × radius**, where the radius is half the width across the funnel's mouth. This works because 1 ml is 1 cubic centimetre, so ml ÷ area gives depth in centimetres, and × 10 turns centimetres into millimetres.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a funnel gauge
blocks.context: For example, Hadiza in Minna uses a funnel 15 cm across its mouth fitted into a 1.5-litre bottle. After a night storm she pours the water into a measuring jug.
steps: Radius = 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 cm.
Funnel area = 3.14 × 7.5 × 7.5 = 176.6 square centimetres (rounded).
Water collected: 530 ml.
She writes "14 June, 30 mm, storm at night" in her log and empties the bottle.
blocks.result: A 30 mm night storm is a heavy rain for one night. When she checks her log at the end of the season, she can count how many nights like this occurred and whether they are becoming more common.

blocks.text: Placing and reading the gauge

items: Put the gauge in an open place, away from roofs, walls and trees. A simple rule: keep it at least as far from any obstacle as that obstacle is tall.
Fix it firmly so wind, goats or children cannot knock it over: tie it to a short post or set it in a tin of sand, with the top about 30 cm above the ground to avoid splashes.
Read it at the same time every morning, for example 7 am, and record the rain that fell over the last 24 hours.
Empty and dry it after every reading. Cover the opening of any stored water and never leave water standing, so mosquitoes cannot breed.
Write 0 on dry days. A zero is a reading too, and dry runs are as important as rainy days.

blocks.text: Adding temperature

A simple indoor and outdoor thermometer from a pharmacy or electronics shop lets you record heat. Read it in the shade, never in direct sun, at the same time each day, such as 3 pm, the hottest part of most days. Write both outdoor shade temperature and the temperature inside your sleeping room at bedtime. These readings will be used in the next lesson on heat.
Turning a month of readings into information

At the end of each month, work out three numbers: the **total rainfall** (add all readings), the number of **rainy days** (for your log, count a day as rainy if 1 mm or more fell), and the **longest dry run** (the most days in a row with less than 1 mm). Those three numbers tell you more than the total alone.

blocks.title: The monthly logging cycle
items: Read gauge every morning
Write mm and notes
Total at month end
Compare with forecast
Share with group
blocks.caption: Repeating the same simple routine every month is what turns readings into a trustworthy record.

blocks.title: Worked example: Hadiza's June summary
blocks.context: For example, Hadiza's June log has 30 daily readings. The days with rain were: 2 June 12 mm, 5 June 3 mm, 12 June 25 mm, 13 June 8 mm, 16 June 0.5 mm, 18 June 14 mm, 26 June 30 mm, 27 June 6 mm, 30 June 2 mm. All other days were 0.
steps: Rainy days (1 mm or more): 2, 5, 12, 13, 18, 26, 27 and 30 June = 8 days. The 0.5 mm on 16 June does not count.
Dry runs: 19 to 25 June is 7 days in a row with no rain. 6 to 11 June is 6 days. The longest dry run is 7 days.
She compares this with her notes from last June and with the dry spell warning in the seasonal forecast for her state.
blocks.result: June had about 100 mm of rain but only 8 rainy days and a 7-day dry run in the middle of the month. For her vegetable plot she now knows to mulch and water during runs of more than five dry days.

blocks.text: Linking your log to the official seasonal forecast

The Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) publishes a Seasonal Climate Prediction early each year. Four of its terms are worth knowing. **Onset**: the expected start of the rainy season. **Cessation**: the expected end. **Length of season**: the days between onset and cessation. **Dry spell**: a run of dry days within the rainy season. When you write your own onset date, cessation date and longest dry runs each year, you can check how well the forecast matched your area, and build your community's trust in using it.

blocks.title: Share the work
blocks.text: A women's group can run one gauge and take turns reading it, with one notebook kept by the secretary. Post the monthly summary in your group's WhatsApp so everyone sees it.

takeaways: Rain is measured as depth in millimetres; container width does not matter if sides are straight
Funnel gauge: mm = ml ÷ (3.14 × radius × radius) × 10
Read at the same time daily, record zeros, and empty the gauge to stop mosquitoes
Monthly: total rain, rainy days of 1 mm or more, and longest dry run
Compare your onset, cessation and dry spells with NiMet's seasonal forecast

activity.title: Build your gauge and log one week
steps: Make a straight-sided or funnel gauge from a clean container.
Place and secure it in an open spot about 30 cm above the ground.
Read it at the same time every morning for seven days, writing zero on dry days.
If you have a thermometer, record the 3 pm shade temperature and bedtime room temperature.
At the end of the week, calculate the total rain, rainy days and longest dry run.
activity.evidence: A photo of your gauge in place and your seven-day log with the three summary numbers

lessons.title: Heat, health and inclusion: protecting the people most at risk in hot seasons
objectives: List the groups most at risk from extreme heat
Recognise the signs of heat exhaustion and heatstroke and give correct first aid
Make a home cooler with low-cost changes
Organise a neighbourhood heat check rota that includes everyone

blocks.text: Floods are easy to see. Heat is quieter, but it is also dangerous. As the planet warms, very hot days and hot nights become more common. The World Health Organization (WHO) warns that heatstroke is a medical emergency, and that some groups are at much higher risk. Women are often among them, for example when cooking indoors over a fire in hot weather.

blocks.name: overheated-face
blocks.alt: A face red and sweating from heat
blocks.caption: Heat illness can come on quietly, so learn the signs before the hot season starts.

blocks.text: Who is most at risk

items: **Older people**, especially over 65, as WHO highlights. Their bodies sense thirst and heat less well.
**Babies and young children**, who heat up quickly and depend on adults for water and shade.
**Pregnant women**.
**People with long-term illnesses** such as heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease or breathing problems, and people with disabilities who may not be able to move to a cooler place alone.
**Outdoor workers**: farmers, market traders, hawkers, okada riders, builders.
**Families in hot, crowded housing** with little airflow, such as rooms with metal roofs and one small window.

blocks.text: WHO's personal advice in hot weather

items: Avoid going outside and doing hard physical work during the hottest time of the day.
Drink water regularly. WHO suggests about 1 cup of water per hour and at least 2 to 3 litres per day. Do not wait until you feel thirsty.
Check regularly on vulnerable people around you, especially those over 65.
Pay attention to alerts and advice from local authorities during hot spells.

blocks.text: Know the danger signs

head: Heat exhaustion
Heatstroke (emergency)
rows: Tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling sick or vomiting, heavy sweating, pale and clammy skin, cramps, great thirst
Very high temperature, hot skin that may stop sweating, fast heartbeat, fast breathing, confusion, poor coordination, fits, collapse
Move to a cool, shady place; remove extra clothing; give water to sip; sponge or spray the skin with cool water and fan
Get emergency help at once (nearest health facility, or call 112); cool the person with water and fanning while you wait
Should feel better within about 30 minutes; if not, treat as heatstroke
If the person becomes unconscious, lay them on their side in the recovery position and keep checking breathing

blocks.title: Do not give drinks to someone who is not fully awake
blocks.text: A person who is confused, very drowsy or unconscious may choke. Cool them and get help instead. Never give medicines for heat illness without a health worker's advice.

blocks.title: Responding to a person struggling in the heat
items: Spot the signs
Move to shade
Cool with water and fan
Sips if fully awake
No better in 30 minutes: emergency
blocks.caption: Act early: cooling at the exhaustion stage can stop it becoming heatstroke.

blocks.text: Keeping the home cooler for little money

items: Close curtains or hang a damp cloth over windows on the sunny side during the day; open windows and doors on opposite sides at night to let air flow through.
Cook outside in a shaded, well-aired spot or very early in the morning, so the house does not fill with heat and smoke.
Let the hottest-affected people, such as an older relative or a baby, sleep in the coolest room, often the one with two windows or under a ceiling.
Use a damp cloth on the neck and wrists, and cool (not icy) baths or sponging before sleep.

blocks.title: Generators on hot nights
blocks.text: Many families run a generator at night for a fan. Never run a generator indoors, on a closed veranda or near a window or door. Its exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill sleeping people.
Inclusion: a heat check rota

The people most at risk are often the least able to ask for help. A **heat check rota** gives each volunteer a short list of named neighbours to visit or call during a hot spell, at a fixed time, with a simple checklist: Do they have water within reach? Are they in the coolest place? Any danger signs? Who will they call if they feel unwell?

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a heat check rota
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's women's group in a Kano neighbourhood lists 14 people at high risk: 9 older people living alone or with only children, 3 pregnant women and 2 people with disabilities. Five members volunteer.
steps: People per volunteer: 14 ÷ 5 = 2.8, so four volunteers take 3 people each and one takes 2 (4 × 3 + 2 = 14).
Checks per day during a hot spell: twice, at about 11 am and 4 pm, so 14 × 2 = 28 checks a day across the group.
Each volunteer makes at most 3 × 2 = 6 checks a day. A phone call takes about 3 minutes and a visit about 10 minutes.
For a 5-day hot spell the group makes 28 × 5 = 140 checks in total.
Each volunteer's list includes the person's name, address, phone number, a family contact and the nearest health facility.
blocks.result: Kemi's group can cover every high-risk neighbour twice a day with no volunteer spending more than about an hour. They agree that any danger sign means calling the family contact and the health facility straight away.

blocks.title: Ask before you list
blocks.text: Get each person's agreement before writing their name or health needs on a rota, and keep the list private within the volunteers. Never post it in a large WhatsApp group.

takeaways: Older people, babies, pregnant women, the chronically ill, people with disabilities and outdoor workers face the most heat risk
WHO advice: avoid the midday heat, drink regularly (about 2 to 3 litres a day), check on vulnerable people
Heat exhaustion: cool, rest, water; heatstroke: emergency help, cool, no drinks if not fully awake
Shade by day, cross-ventilate at night, cook outside, never run a generator indoors
A heat check rota protects people who cannot ask for help

activity.title: Make your household and street heat plan
steps: Write the names of everyone in your household and circle anyone in a high-risk group.
Choose the coolest room and decide who sleeps there during hot spells.
Copy the danger-signs table and stick it where everyone can see it.
Identify at least three high-risk neighbours and, with their permission, agree a check-in time with them.
Save the number of the nearest health facility and 112 in your phone.
activity.evidence: A photo of your posted danger-signs sheet and a note of your coolest room and three agreed check-ins

lessons.title: Measuring progress: tracking fuel, water and household climate actions
objectives: Choose four or five honest indicators for your climate actions
Record a baseline and compare it with later results
Calculate percentage change and money saved from your own records
Use WHO's list of clean cooking options to plan a cleaner kitchen

blocks.text: Good intentions do not prove that anything changed. **Measuring** does. In this lesson you choose a few simple indicators, record where you start (the **baseline**), make one change, and measure again. The example focuses on cooking fuel, because it touches three things at once: money, health and greenhouse gases.

blocks.name: growth-chart
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a rising bar chart
blocks.caption: Numbers written before and after a change show whether it worked.

blocks.text: Why the kitchen matters

WHO reports that about 2.1 billion people worldwide cook with open fires or inefficient stoves using kerosene, wood, charcoal, dung, crop waste or coal. The smoke causes heart disease, stroke, lung infections and lung disease, and WHO notes that women and children, who usually cook and collect firewood, bear the greatest health burden. Using less wood and charcoal also means fewer trees cut and less money spent.

WHO counts these as **clean** cooking options: solar, electricity, biogas, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG, cooking gas), natural gas, alcohol fuels, and biomass stoves that meet WHO's emission targets. If you cannot switch fully yet, using less charcoal or wood with a better stove and good habits is still a step forward.
Habits that cut fuel use

items: Keep a lid on the pot. Food boils faster and uses less fuel.
Soak beans and hard grains for several hours before cooking.
Use dry wood or charcoal and keep the stove sheltered from wind.
Turn down the heat once food boils: a gentle simmer cooks just as well.

**Retained-heat cooking**: bring a pot of beans, rice or stew to the boil, then place the closed pot in an insulated basket or a box packed with cloths or dry grass. It keeps cooking slowly with no extra fuel. Reheat to boiling before serving if it has cooled.

blocks.title: Smoke and fire safety
blocks.text: Cook in a well-ventilated place, keep babies and young children away from smoke and hot pots, and never bring a burning or glowing charcoal stove into a closed room, because charcoal also produces carbon monoxide. Keep a bucket of sand or water nearby when cooking with fire.
Choosing indicators

An **indicator** is something you can count or measure that shows whether a practice is working. Choose only four or five, so you can keep recording them every week. Each needs a unit, a method and a baseline.

head: Indicator
Unit and method
Example baseline
rows: kg per week, weighed with a market scale or counted in tins of known weight
Naira per week, from receipts or notebook
Days of supply: litres stored ÷ litres the household drinks per day

blocks.title: Measuring a change honestly
items: Record baseline for four weeks
Make one change
Record four more weeks
Calculate the difference
Keep, adjust or drop
blocks.caption: Changing one thing at a time lets you see what really caused the result.

blocks.title: Worked example: did the retained-heat basket save charcoal?
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Ibadan cooks for six people with charcoal. She weighs the charcoal she uses each week for four weeks, then starts using a lid on every pot and a retained-heat basket for beans and stews, and weighs again for four weeks. For this example she pays about ₦700 per kg of charcoal; prices vary by place and season.
steps: Before: 9, 8.5, 9.5 and 9 kg. Average = (9 + 8.5 + 9.5 + 9) ÷ 4 = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 kg per week.
After: 7, 6.5, 7 and 6.5 kg. Average = 27 ÷ 4 = 6.75 kg per week.
Saving: 9 - 6.75 = 2.25 kg per week.
Percentage change: 2.25 ÷ 9 × 100 = 25% less charcoal.
Money saved: 2.25 × ₦700 = about ₦1,575 per week; over 52 weeks about ₦81,900 a year at that price.
blocks.result: In Funke's own kitchen, the lid and basket cut charcoal use by a quarter. She keeps the practice, shows her neighbours her notebook, and starts saving the weekly difference towards a two-burner gas cooker.

blocks.text: Reading your results honestly

If a number did not move, ask why. Was it a festival week with extra cooking? Did the charcoal quality change? Record the reason next to the number. Compare like with like: four ordinary weeks against four ordinary weeks. And remember that one household's result is evidence for that household. When several families measure and get similar results, you have a stronger case to share with your community or a partner organisation.

blocks.title: Days of water supply
blocks.text: To calculate days of drinking water stored, divide litres stored by litres drunk per day. For example, a household of five drinking about 2.5 litres each uses about 12.5 litres a day, so a 50-litre covered container holds 50 ÷ 12.5 = 4 days of drinking water.

takeaways: Measure a baseline before you change anything
Choose four or five indicators with a unit and a method
Percentage change = difference ÷ baseline × 100
Lids, soaking, gentle simmering and retained-heat cooking cut fuel use; WHO lists LPG, electricity, biogas and solar among clean options
Never bring a glowing charcoal stove into a closed room

activity.title: Start your indicator sheet
steps: Pick four or five indicators from this lesson or your own vulnerabilities.
Write the unit and how you will measure each one.
Record your baseline this week for each indicator.
Choose one change to test for the next four weeks, such as lids and a retained-heat basket.
Set a date to calculate the difference and percentage change.
activity.evidence: Your indicator sheet with units, methods, baseline values and the dated change you will test

quiz.q: Hadiza's funnel is 10 cm across. After a storm she collects 393 ml. About how much rain fell?
quiz.explain: Radius 5 cm, area = 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 square cm. 393 ÷ 78.5 × 10 = about 50 mm.

quiz.q: Why should a rain gauge be emptied after every reading and kept covered when not in use?
options: Because rain water is always poisonous
So each reading covers only 24 hours and mosquitoes cannot breed in standing water
quiz.explain: Emptying keeps readings accurate for one day at a time, and removing standing water prevents mosquito breeding.

quiz.q: An older neighbour is confused, has hot skin and a fast heartbeat on a very hot afternoon. What should Kemi do first?
options: Give her a large cup of water to drink quickly
Tell her to rest and check again tomorrow
Get emergency help at once and cool her with water and fanning while waiting
quiz.explain: Confusion with hot skin and fast heartbeat are heatstroke signs, a medical emergency. Do not give drinks to someone confused, and never give medicines without a health worker.

quiz.q: A family runs a generator at night to power a fan. Where should it be?
options: Outdoors, well away from windows and doors
Inside the parlour so it is not stolen
Next to the bedroom window for a short cable
quiz.explain: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can kill sleeping people. It must run outdoors, far from openings.

quiz.q: Funke used 9 kg of charcoal per week before and 6.3 kg after a change. What is the percentage reduction?
Which of these does WHO list as a clean cooking option?
quiz.explain: WHO lists solar, electricity, biogas, LPG, natural gas, alcohol fuels and biomass stoves meeting its emission targets as clean. Kerosene and open fires are polluting.

modules.title: Leading Climate Action in Your Community
modules.overview: You turn what you have learned into visible community action with trees, shade and clear drains, learn to talk about climate change clearly and work with the right partners, and complete your capstone project with an honest record and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: From knowledge to action: trees, shade and clear drains in your community
objectives: Explain how trees and clear drains reduce heat, erosion and flooding
Plan a small tree-planting effort that keeps seedlings alive
Calculate seedling survival rate and replacements needed
Organise a safe drain clean-up with neighbours

blocks.text: Some of the best climate actions are also the oldest: planting and caring for trees, and keeping water flowing where it should. These are called **nature-based solutions** because they use living things and natural processes to protect people. They work for adaptation and mitigation at the same time: a tree shades a compound today and takes carbon dioxide out of the air as it grows.

blocks.name: nature-benefits
blocks.alt: A person relaxing among trees and plants
blocks.caption: Trees around homes, schools and markets give shade, hold soil and store carbon.

blocks.text: What trees and clear drains do

items: **Shade and cooling**: a shade tree near a house, school or market stall makes the space under it cooler, which helps the heat-sensitive people from Module 2.
**Holding soil**: roots bind the soil, and leaves soften heavy raindrops, so less soil washes away. Planting and protecting vegetation is a key part of controlling erosion around gullies and slopes.
**Windbreaks**: rows of trees slow dry winds and dust, which matters in the north during harmattan.

**Clear drains**: in towns, a great deal of flooding after heavy rain happens because drains are blocked with plastic bags, bottles and other waste. Water that cannot flow away rises into streets, shops and homes.

blocks.text: Planting so trees survive
Planting a seedling takes ten minutes; keeping it alive takes two years. Many planting days fail because nobody waters or protects the young trees. Plan for care from the start.

items: Choose the right tree for the place and purpose. Ask your State Ministry of Environment, the state forestry office or a local nursery which species grow well in your zone and suit shade, fruit or erosion control.
Plant at the start of the rainy season, once the soil is properly moist, so roots establish before the dry season.
Dig a hole about twice as wide as the root ball. Remove the polythene bag carefully without breaking the soil around the roots.
Set the seedling at the same depth it was in the bag, fill with soil, press firmly and water well.
Mulch around the base with dry leaves or grass, leaving a small gap at the stem.
Protect it from goats and people with a ring of sticks, an old basket or a thorny branch.
Assign each tree to a named caretaker who waters it during dry spells and the first dry season.

blocks.title: A tree's first year
items: Plan species and caretakers
Plant at early rains
Weekly checks in rainy season
Water through dry season
Count survivors, replace losses
blocks.caption: The work after planting decides whether the trees live.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting tree survival
blocks.context: For example, Blessing's women's group plants 60 shade and fruit seedlings around a primary school in Jos, with 12 members each caring for 5 trees. For this example seedlings cost about ₦300 each at a local nursery; prices vary.
steps: Cost of seedlings: 60 × ₦300 = about ₦18,000.
After three months, they count 42 living trees.
Survival rate: 42 ÷ 60 × 100 = 70%.
Trees lost: 60 - 42 = 18. Most losses were on the side next to the football field, where children trampled them.
Replacement cost: 18 × ₦300 = about ₦5,400. They replant at the next rains and add stick rings on that side.
blocks.result: Blessing's group learns that protection was the weak point, not watering. They record the survival rate and the reason, and set a target of at least 85% survival for the replanted trees.

blocks.text: A safe drain clean-up

Drain clearing works best before the heavy rains and as a regular routine, not only after a flood. Talk to your local government area's sanitation or environment office first: they may lend tools, arrange waste collection and tell you which drains are their responsibility.

blocks.title: Protect the people doing the work
blocks.text: Wear thick gloves and boots, cover cuts, and do not let children help in drains. Never enter a drain or gutter during rain or when water is flowing. Lift heavy slabs with several people and proper tools. Wash hands well with soap and water afterwards. Waste from drains can carry germs and sharp objects, so bag it and arrange collection; do not burn it, because burning plastic gives off harmful smoke.

Prevention matters more than clearing. Agree with traders and households on where waste goes, and ask the LGA about regular collection. Some groups also sort clean plastic bottles and sachets for local recyclers who buy them, which can turn a cost into a small income.

blocks.title: Start where people already gather
blocks.text: A school, market, church, mosque or health centre gives you a place everyone uses, a group already organised, and a reason for others to help look after the trees or drains.

takeaways: Trees give shade, hold soil, slow wind and store carbon
Plant at early rains, mulch, protect, and assign a caretaker to every tree
Survival rate = living trees ÷ trees planted × 100
Blocked drains cause much urban flooding; clear them safely before the rains and prevent waste from entering

activity.title: Plan one nature-based action
steps: Choose either tree planting or a drain clean-up for your street, compound, school or market.
Write who you will ask for advice or support (nursery, forestry office, LGA sanitation office).
List the people involved and give each a named task.
Write the safety rules you will follow.
Set a date and decide what you will count afterwards (trees alive, metres of drain cleared, bags of waste removed).
activity.evidence: A one-page action plan with date, people, tasks, safety rules and what you will count

lessons.title: Talking about climate change and building partnerships that last
objectives: Explain climate change to a community group in under ten minutes without jargon
Respond respectfully to common misunderstandings
Identify the right public bodies and local partners for your project
Write a specific request to a partner

blocks.text: People act on what they understand and trust. A good climate conversation starts from what listeners have already seen with their own eyes, explains the cause simply, and ends with one thing they can do this week. Long lists of global facts usually lose an audience.

blocks.name: conference-speaker
blocks.alt: A woman speaking to a small audience
blocks.caption: A short, local talk at a meeting people already attend reaches more people than a long event.

blocks.text: A ten-minute talk that works

blocks.title: Shape of a short climate talk
items: A change everyone noticed
What causes it
What it means here
One action to try
A clear ask
blocks.caption: Moving from local experience to a single action keeps the talk practical and memorable.

blocks.title: Worked example: Zainab's talk at a women's meeting
blocks.context: For example, Zainab has ten minutes at her market women's association meeting in Kaduna. She plans each part in minutes.
steps: Minutes 0 to 2, local change: "Who remembers when the rains started in April? This year we waited until May." She shows her seasonal calendar photo from Module 1.
Minutes 2 to 4, cause: the greenhouse effect in three sentences, using the wrapper-on-a-baby picture.
Minutes 4 to 7, what it means here, plus one action: hotter afternoons in the market. She shows the heat danger signs and the WHO advice on drinking water regularly.
Minutes 7 to 9, questions from members.
Minutes 9 to 10, the ask: "Write your name here if you will check on one older trader in the next hot spell."
Total: 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 minutes.
blocks.result: Eleven members sign up for the market heat rota. Zainab writes the number down as her result and plans a follow-up talk on clear drains before the rains.

blocks.text: Common misunderstandings and respectful answers

head: What someone may say
A respectful reply
rows: "It is just a bad year, things will go back to normal."
"Maybe. Let us check our records. If the change keeps showing year after year, it is safer to plan for it."
"Climate change is a problem for rich countries."
"They have produced more of the gases, but we are already feeling the effects here: later rains, hotter days. Preparing protects our own families."
"There is nothing ordinary people can do."
"We cannot stop it alone, but we can reduce the harm: store water, check on older people, plant and protect trees, keep drains clear."
Listen and show respect. Focus on shared values such as caring for neighbours and protecting children, and on practical steps everyone can agree on.

blocks.title: Use people's own words
blocks.text: Translate key ideas into your local language. "Heat that stays in the air" is often clearer than "greenhouse effect". Check with one or two listeners afterwards that the message was understood.
Who to partner with

Nigeria's **Climate Change Act, 2021** established the **National Council on Climate Change (NCCC)** as the apex body for climate matters in the country. Most practical help, though, comes from people closer to you.

items: **State Ministry of Environment and the LGA environment or sanitation office**: waste collection, drain clearing, tree planting programmes.
**Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) extension workers**: advice on crops and seasons for farming families.
**Primary health centre staff**: support for heat safety messages and the heat check rota.
**NiMet**: the seasonal forecast and weather warnings to share with your group.
**Schools, religious groups, market associations and cooperatives**: places, people and trust.
**Registered NGOs working on environment or women's livelihoods in your state**: check they are genuine before sharing any personal data or money.

blocks.text: Making a specific request

Partners respond better to a clear, small, specific request than to "please help us with climate change". Say who you are, what you have already done, exactly what you need, for how many people, and by when.

items: Introduce your group and its members in one sentence.
Show what you have already done, with numbers: "We planted 60 trees; 42 survived."
State the exact request: "Can your office supply 20 replacement seedlings and stick guards before 15 May?"
Say what you will do in return: "We will water them and send you a survival count after three months."
Give a contact name and phone number, and follow up within one week.

blocks.text: Make communication two-way

Partnerships last longer when information flows in both directions. Do not only receive forecasts and advice: send back what your community observes. A monthly message to your extension worker or LGA environment officer with your rain log summary (total rain, rainy days, longest dry run), any flooding of streets or drains, and how many people your heat rota reached gives them local evidence they rarely have. Keep the message short, with dates and numbers, and keep copies. Over a year, these reports show partners that your group is organised and reliable, which makes the next request easier to grant.

blocks.title: Watch for scams
blocks.text: Be careful of anyone who asks your group to pay a fee to receive "climate grants" or "green funds". Genuine agencies do not ask for payment through personal accounts. Verify any offer directly with the agency's official office before sharing money or members' details.

takeaways: Start from a change people have seen, explain the cause simply, end with one action and one ask
Answer misunderstandings with records and shared values, not arguments
The Climate Change Act, 2021 established the National Council on Climate Change
Local partners include the LGA, State Ministry of Environment, ADP, health centre, NiMet and community groups
A good request is small, specific, time-bound and shows what you have already done

activity.title: Plan your talk and one request
steps: Write a ten-minute talk plan using the five parts, with minutes for each.
Choose one misunderstanding you expect and write your respectful reply.
Deliver the talk to a group you belong to, or to your family.
Write one specific request to a local partner using the five steps.
Record how many people took the action you asked for.
activity.evidence: Your talk plan, a note of how many people attended and acted, and a copy of your written request

lessons.title: Your community climate resilience project and 90-day plan
objectives: Put together your capstone: risk assessment, one documented practice and a 90-day plan
Report results honestly, including what did not work
Rescore your household vulnerability to show change
Write a 90-day plan with dated milestones and measurable targets

blocks.text: This lesson brings the course together. Your capstone shows three things: that you understand your local climate risks, that you have actually done something about one of them, and that you have a realistic plan to keep going. It does not need to be big. One practice done well and measured honestly is worth more than five half-started ideas.

blocks.name: project-completed
blocks.alt: A person ticking off a completed project board
blocks.caption: A finished project is one you can show with evidence, not just describe.

blocks.text: The three parts of your capstone

head: Part
What to include
Where it comes from
rows: Your zone, three local climate signals, your five-area scoring sheet and top three vulnerabilities
What you did and why, dates, people involved, your indicators with baseline and results, photos, what worked and what did not
How you will extend the practice or start a partnership, with dated milestones, targets and who is responsible

blocks.text: Writing up your results honestly

Readers trust a report that admits problems. For each result, give the number, the comparison with your baseline, and the reason you think it changed. If something failed, say what happened and what you changed. "Our first rota missed two people because we had no phone numbers; we fixed this in week two" shows real learning.

items: Use numbers you measured yourself, with units.
Show before and after, not after alone.
Separate what you saw from what you think caused it.
Get permission before including photos or names of neighbours, and leave out private health details.

blocks.title: Worked example: Rahila's project summary
blocks.context: For example, Rahila lives in Lafia and sells pepper and tomatoes. Her top vulnerability in Module 1 was income (score 9): heavy rain flooded her stall, and hot afternoons made her and two older traders beside her unwell.
steps: Practice chosen: raising her stock on a wooden platform and organising a heat check rota for 9 older traders in her market line, run by 3 traders, each covering 3 people.
Baseline (4 weeks before): about 2 baskets of tomatoes spoiled by flood water; no one checking on older traders.
Results (8 weeks after): no stock lost to flooding in 3 heavy rains (her gauge showed 25, 32 and 41 mm). Rota checks: 9 people × 2 checks × 6 hot days = 108 checks planned; 96 made.
Rota completion: 96 ÷ 108 × 100 = about 89%. Missed checks were on a market holiday; they now agree cover in advance.
Rescore for income: exposure 3, sensitivity 2 (stock protected), capacity gap 2 (a small emergency saving started). Total 3 + 2 + 2 = 7, down from 9.
blocks.result: Rahila's summary shows a measured fall in her vulnerability score from 9 to 7, a working heat rota and an honest gap she has fixed. It is concrete, checkable and realistic.

blocks.text: Building your 90-day plan

A 90-day plan turns one success into a habit. Choose **one** direction: reach more households with the same practice, add a second practice, or formalise a partnership. Break the 90 days into milestones about two to four weeks apart, each with a target number and a named person.

blocks.title: A 90-day plan in four milestones
items: Day 1-14: recruit and train
Day 15-45: run and record
Day 46-75: review and adjust
Day 76-90: report and share
blocks.caption: Each milestone ends with a number you can check.

head: Milestone
Rahila's example target
Who
rows: Rota extended to two more market lines: 18 older traders listed with consent, 6 volunteers trained
At least 85% of planned checks completed; 3 more traders raise stock off the ground
Written request to the market association and LGA for a shaded rest spot and drain clearing
Results shared at the association meeting; rescores collected from 5 traders

blocks.title: Keep it small enough to finish
blocks.text: If a target feels too big, halve it. A plan you complete builds trust with your community and partners; a plan you abandon makes the next one harder.
Presenting your file

Keep your capstone short and easy to share. A good format is a one-page summary at the front, then your evidence behind it: the calendar photo, scoring sheets, indicator sheet and plan. The one-page summary should answer five questions in plain sentences: What is our main climate risk? What did we do? What changed, in numbers? What went wrong and how did we respond? What will we do in the next 90 days? A summary like this can be read aloud at a meeting, sent as photos on WhatsApp, or attached to a request to a partner. Store the original notebook pages safely, because next year's comparisons depend on them.
Final check before you submit

items: Top three vulnerabilities named, with scores.
One practice with dates, baseline, results and photos.
At least one honest problem and how you responded.
A rescore showing what changed.
A 90-day plan with milestones, numbers and names.

takeaways: Your capstone has three parts: risk assessment, one documented practice, a 90-day plan
Report numbers you measured, before and after, and name what went wrong
Rescore your vulnerability to show real change
A 90-day plan needs milestones, targets and named people
Small and finished beats big and abandoned

activity.title: Draft your capstone
steps: Gather your notebook, calendar photo, scoring sheet and indicator sheet.
Write your project summary using Rahila's structure: practice, baseline, results, problem, rescore.
Calculate at least one percentage or change in score with your own numbers.
Write a 90-day plan with four dated milestones, targets and names.
Share the draft with one group member and ask what is unclear.
activity.evidence: Your capstone draft with all three parts and a note of the feedback you received

quiz.q: Blessing's group planted 80 seedlings and 60 are alive after three months. What is the survival rate?
Why do many tree-planting days fail?
options: Planting is done at the start of the rains
Nobody waters or protects the young trees after planting
quiz.explain: Care after planting decides survival. Each tree needs protection and a named caretaker, especially through the first dry season.

quiz.q: During a heavy rain, a neighbour wants to climb into the blocked gutter to clear it. What is the right advice?
options: Never enter a drain while water is flowing; clear it safely with gloves and boots when it is dry
Go ahead quickly before it overflows
Burn the waste in the drain
Send the children in because they are small
quiz.explain: Flowing water in drains can sweep people away and carries germs. Clearing is done before the rains, with protective gear, never by children.

quiz.q: Which is the best request to a partner?
options: Please help us with climate change
We planted 60 trees and 42 survived. Can your office supply 20 seedlings and stick guards before 15 May? We will send a survival count in three months.
quiz.explain: A good request shows what you have done, asks for something specific, gives a date and says what you will do in return.

quiz.q: Rahila planned 108 rota checks and made 96. What is the completion rate?
Someone in your group receives a message offering a "green fund grant" if the group pays a processing fee into a personal account. What should you do?
options: Pay quickly before the offer ends
Share members' phone numbers to speed it up
Treat it as a likely scam and verify directly with the agency's official office
quiz.explain: Genuine agencies do not ask for fees through personal accounts. Verify any offer with the official office first.

finalQuiz.q: What is the main difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is in the north, climate is in the south
Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the average pattern over about 30 years
They mean exactly the same thing
finalQuiz.explain: WMO uses 30-year averages, called climate normals, to describe climate.

finalQuiz.q: According to the United Nations, what has been the main driver of climate change since the 1800s?
options: Human activities, mainly burning coal, oil and gas
finalQuiz.explain: The UN states human activities, primarily burning fossil fuels, have been the main driver.

finalQuiz.q: A community plants trees that store carbon and also shade a market. This action is:
finalQuiz.explain: Shade reduces heat harm (adaptation) and growing trees take carbon dioxide from the air (mitigation).

finalQuiz.q: A coastal community reports that well water has turned salty and farmland near the creek is failing. Which climate concern fits best?
finalQuiz.explain: Sea water reaching wells and farmland is saltwater intrusion, a typical coastal concern.

finalQuiz.q: Which household area should get attention first: water (total 5), income (8), health (7), food (6), housing (4)?
finalQuiz.explain: The highest total shows the greatest vulnerability. Income at 8 comes first.

finalQuiz.q: A straight-sided bucket left in the open overnight holds water 18 mm deep. How much rain fell?
options: It depends on the bucket width
finalQuiz.explain: For a straight-sided container, water depth equals rainfall, whatever the width.

finalQuiz.q: In a June log the readings show the longest run of days below 1 mm was 9 days in mid-June. What does this show?
options: A dry spell inside the rainy season
finalQuiz.explain: A run of dry days within the rainy season is a dry spell, a term used in NiMet's seasonal forecast.

finalQuiz.q: WHO's advice on drinking water in hot weather is:
options: Drink water regularly, about 1 cup per hour and at least 2 to 3 litres a day
Avoid water and drink sugary drinks
finalQuiz.explain: WHO advises regular drinking, about a cup per hour and at least 2 to 3 litres a day, without waiting for thirst.

finalQuiz.q: A trader feels dizzy, sweaty and has cramps on a hot afternoon but is fully alert. What is the best first response?
options: Give her medicine from the market
Move her to shade, loosen extra clothing, give water to sip and cool her skin
Pour very hot water on her
finalQuiz.explain: These are heat exhaustion signs. Cool, rest and water; if not better in about 30 minutes, get emergency help.

finalQuiz.q: A household's weekly charcoal spending falls from ₦8,000 to ₦6,000. What is the percentage saving?
Which law established Nigeria's National Council on Climate Change?
finalQuiz.explain: The NCCC was established by the Climate Change Act, 2021 as the apex body for climate matters in Nigeria.

finalQuiz.q: Which 90-day plan milestone is best written?
options: By day 45, at least 85% of planned heat checks completed for 18 traders; volunteers responsible
finalQuiz.explain: A good milestone has a date, a measurable target and named responsibility.

capstone.title: Community Climate Resilience Project
capstone.brief: Produce a short project file with three parts: a local climate risk assessment naming your household's or community's top three vulnerabilities; documentation of one resilience practice you introduced or strengthened, with baseline, measured results and honest lessons; and a 90-day plan to extend the practice or build a partnership.
steps: Record your zone and three local climate signals from your notebook and seasonal calendar.
Complete the five-area vulnerability scoring sheet and name your top three vulnerabilities.
Choose one practice that addresses a top vulnerability, such as a heat check rota, a rain log, fuel-saving cooking, raised stock, tree care or drain clearing.
Record a baseline, run the practice for at least four weeks, and measure again with your indicators.
Write your results honestly, including one problem and how you responded, and rescore the vulnerability.
Write a 90-day plan with four dated milestones, measurable targets and named people.
Share your file with your group or a partner and note their feedback.
evidence: Seasonal calendar photo and three local climate signals
Completed vulnerability scoring sheet with top three named
Indicator sheet showing baseline and results with units
Photos of the practice in action (with consent)
At least one calculation: percentage change, survival rate or score change
A 90-day plan with milestones, targets and names
